                                     PROJECT NO. 58482
 LARGE LOAD DEMAND                               §       PUBLIC UTILITY COMMISSION
 MANAGEMENT SERVICE                              §                OF TEXAS

              TEXAS INDUSTRIAL ENERGY CONSUMERS’ COMMENTS

                                      I.   INTRODUCTION

       Texas Industrial Energy Consumers (TIEC) appreciates the opportunity to provide

feedback on the implementation of PURA § 39.170(b) and the development of a Large Load

Demand Management Service within the ERCOT market.

       TIEC members are among the large electricity users who proposed this service previously

at the Commission and ultimately as part of Senate Bill (SB 6). Many industrial sites are not

flexible and do not typically participate in the wholesale market but are able to reduce their usage

in advance of an emergency event with notice. This notice allows the users to pre-position site

personnel and adjust site operations to achieve an orderly ramp down over a long period, which is

not currently facilitated by existing services with deployment times at thirty minutes or less. TIEC

envisions this service as formalizing the types of communications and activities that have

historically been done on an ad hoc, voluntary basis with some industrial sites ahead of emergency

conditions. Currently, in anticipation of an extreme weather event, the Commission and ERCOT

will often ask industrial customers to voluntarily curtail during the periods when forecasted

conditions look the tightest. These communications often begin several days before an identifiable

weather event—usually a winter storm, but sometimes extreme summer heat). During Winter




                                                 1
 Storm Elliott in December 2022, 1 Winter Storm Heather in January 2024, 2 and Winter Storm Fern

in January 2026, 3 the Commission and ERCOT acknowledged that this curtailment helped

maintain reliability. While this informal approach has benefits and can continue in parallel, a more

structured service will provide greater assurance that large loads will provide this type of demand

response, will give ERCOT greater transparency into participation, and will help many companies

socialize and explain these activities internally.

         With this context, TIEC envisioned the Large Load Demand Management Service as an

“as-needed” deployment model, where ERCOT would procure participation ahead of an identified

extreme weather event only if needed. TIEC did not envision that the service would be seasonally

contracted like Emergency Response Service (ERS) because there may be some seasons, and even

years, where the service is not needed and would not be procured. This approach best aligns with

what already occurs informally and the Legislature’s intent under PURA § 39.170(b). An event-

driven model should reduce overall costs, tie procurement to real grid needs, and increase

participation by giving large industrial customers flexibility to assess near-term operations, safety,

            GridMonitor, Meeting of the Public Utility Commission of Texas at 00:09:59-00:10:46 (January 29, 2026)
(available at: https://dash2.gridmonitor.com/sharing/?token=*** (“Large

                                                            2
 and business factors closer in time to a potential deployment. For the types of load this service

should attract, a seasonal contract will likely involve a level of speculation and internal forecasting

that may deter participation. Again, these are not flexible loads and not the types of loads that

actively participate in the market today.

       That being said, TIEC is open to ongoing dialogue as to the most cost-effective and

beneficial implementation. While some TIEC members will participate in the service, others will

not and will pay the costs. With this context in mind, TIEC offers preliminary thoughts on

Commission Staff’s questions.


                                        II.    COMMENTS

1.     Of the two options described in the attached slides, an as-needed service or a seasonal
       service, which is the better option to implement PURA § 39.170(b) and why?
       TIEC believes an “as-needed” service better implements PURA § 39.170(b) because it will

only be procured for specific extreme weather events. TIEC also anticipates that this approach

will be more effective, more cost-efficient, and will maximize participation.

       As mentioned previously, a central objective of the Large Load Management Service is to

incentivize participation from large loads that would not otherwise participate in the wholesale

market (including price response or ancillary services), but who are able to voluntarily reduce

demand at ERCOT’s request in advance of emergency conditions. Under PURA § 39.170, the

service should exclude loads that are price-responsive or that participate in other reliability or

ancillary services. 4 In other words, the service should be designed to attract offers from loads that,

by their nature, do not actively participate in the market but may be willing to respond on a case-

by-case, event-specific basis.



       4
           See PURA § 39.170(b)(3).

                                                  3
         An as-needed design is more likely to attract participation from eligible large loads than an

ERS-style service. Many of the large load facilities eligible to provide this service operate complex

facilities where the decision to curtail load involves significant operational, safety, and business

considerations. It is more difficult for these customers to commit to curtailing on a seasonal basis,

potentially months in advance. In many ways, a seasonal large load demand service would be

similar to ERCOT’s Summer 2024 Contracts for Capacity RFP, which was ultimately

unsuccessful. 5 For example, both a seasonal service and the RFP entail non-price responsive loads

providing demand-response as needed for a three-month period. While the RFP did not include a

24-hour notice or extreme weather event requirements, it should be illustrative of the limited

number of loads, much less large loads, that may be interested in providing a seasonal demand

response service and are not already participating in ERS. By contrast, an ad hoc, event-triggered

approach allows customers to more contemporaneously evaluate their specific circumstances—

including production schedules, operational conditions, and contractual obligations. This practical

flexibility will likely result in greater participation.

        Additionally, the as-needed model should be more cost-effective. Because procurement

occurs only when ERCOT identifies a need, there is no standing procurement obligation and

therefore no payments would be made for certain seasons or even years. While it may be efficient

to set an annual budget to create more predictability for REPs (as described below), participating

loads would not receive an around-the-clock payment for availability or standby capacity over the

course of an entire season if the service is not needed. Instead, participating loads would be

compensated only if they actually curtail in response to a specific procurement event. By contrast,


         5
            Energy Choice Matters, ERCOT Cancels Summer Capacity RFP (June 21, 2024) (available at:
https://www.energychoicematters.com/stories/20240621c.html) (explaining that ERCOT only received offers from
two QSEs totaling 21.5 MW of capacity with only 6.5 MW of capacity that could potentially qualify).

                                                     4
 the seasonal model would establish seasonal spend limits and commit resources in advance,

creating budget obligations regardless of whether an emergency event materialized during the

season.

2.        PURA § 39.170(b) states the commission must require ERCOT to develop a reliability
          service to be deployed in the event of an anticipated emergency condition. PURA
          § 39.170(b)(1) states the rules governing the new service must specify the periods
          when the service may be used to assist with maintaining reliability during extreme
          weather events.
          a.        Does PURA authorize ERCOT to deploy the new service in circumstances
                    other than extreme weather events? If yes, what kind of events?

          b.        Should the commission define “extreme weather event” and, if so, how
                    should it be defined?

          PURA § 39.170(b)(1) limits the deployment of the large load management service to

“extreme weather events.” Specifically, PURA states, “the rules governing this service must

specify the periods when the service may be used to assist with maintaining reliability during

extreme weather events.” 6 The directive to “specify the periods when the service may be used”

requires ERCOT to define the particular types of extreme weather events where it may deploy the

service. It is not meant to be a standing tool available at all times or for all categories of grid stress

like other ancillary services but tied to identifiable weather events. Had the Legislature intended

ERCOT to deploy the service in anticipation of any event that may result in entering in an energy

emergency alert, it would not have used such prescriptive language.

          As-needed procurement ahead of an identified weather event (likely an extreme winter

storm) is also the best policy for customers. The ERCOT market already includes a range of

ancillary services and reliability mechanisms designed to address non-weather-related

contingencies.        Extending this new reliability service to those scenarios would effectively



          6
              PURA § 39.170(b) (emphasis added).

                                                    5
 repurpose it for conditions that existing market tools are better suited to address. This program’s

intended participants—large industrial loads with significant curtailment lead times and complex

restart procedures—are not well-positioned to serve as a resource for the full range of reliability

events that may arise on the ERCOT system. Confining the service to extreme weather events

preserves a clear and workable boundary to avoid undermining the effectiveness of the service by

overextending its scope and deterring participation.

       At the onset of this program, it would be reasonable to define “extreme weather events” at

least initially, as extreme winter storms. Unlike summer heat, which is predictable, persistent and

well-suited for other types of market response, winter weather events pose the greatest reliability

risk today and are typically discrete and identifiable. A major winter storm is typically identifiable

in weather forecasts well in advance, facilitating the 24-hour advance notice period contemplated

by the program’s design. Large load customers can plan for and execute an orderly curtailment

when a named or forecasted winter storm is approaching in a way that is not feasible for other, less

predictable reliability events. Further, this type of a bright-line more limited standard would help

ensure that the service is reserved for genuinely extreme conditions and is not diluted through

routine deployment during summer heat.

       TIEC is open to using the service for other types of events, but as an initial step, winter

weather events appear the most suitable. The service could be expanded to other scenarios once

the Commission and ERCOT gain operational experience and develop a clearer understanding of

the system’s needs, customer responsiveness, curtailment capabilities, and pricing dynamics.

3.     PURA § 39.170(b)(3) states the rules governing the new service must prohibit
       participation by any large load customer that curtails in response to the wholesale
       price of electricity, as determined by ERCOT, or that otherwise participates in a
       different reliability or ancillary service. PURA § 37.0561(e)—which allows ERCOT
       to direct a large load customer with onsite backup generation to either curtail its load

                                                  6
        or deploy its backup generation under certain circumstances—states that a large load
       customer with onsite backup generation may participate in a service authorized by
       PURA § 39.170(b).
       a.      What type of qualification is necessary to show that it may take a large load
               customer 24 hours to ramp down safely?

       b.      What specific prohibitions not enumerated in PURA § 39.170(b), if any,
               should apply to participation in the new service?

       c.      Should participation in price responsiveness to transmission scarcity such as
               four coincident peak (4CP) or a successor methodology preclude
               participation in the new service?

       d.      Should the commission define “curtailment in response to wholesale price of
               electricity” and, if so, how should it be defined?

       TIEC does not believe it is necessary for a load to show that it takes a full twenty-four

hours to ramp down safely in order to participate. PURA § 39.170(b)(2) requires ERCOT to

provide at least 24 hours’ advance notice before deployment, but the statute itself does not require

a 24-hour ramp-down period. In many instances, the actual curtailment will not take twenty-four

hours, but preparatory site activities need to be initiated up to 24-hours in advance. This advance

notice will allow industrial facilities to deploy additional personnel and initiate processes that

allow a reduction in load without compromising safety, product quality, or equipment integrity.

Further, the requirement that participating loads cannot otherwise be price responsive or participate

in ancillary service markets will naturally exclude loads with shorter curtailment capabilities,

driving them into other markets. Consistent with that purpose, qualification should focus on

whether the load can reduce consumption with advance notice to reach the committed curtailment

level safely. This could be memorialized through limited testing or enrollment with a Qualified

Scheduling Entity (QSE) and a straightforward attestation that the site has a protocol in place to

meet the program’s deployment parameters. Again, if the service is only compensated based on

actual curtailments, there is no need for the kind of rigorous eligibility requirements used for other

ancillary or reliability services that receive advance capacity payments.
                                                  7
        To determine whether a load “curtails in response to the wholesale price of electricity” and

is prohibited from participating in the service, ERCOT should look for a pattern of significant

price-response and not isolated instances. In ERCOT’s Summer 2024 Contracts for Capacity

Governing Document, ERCOT determined that a site was price-responsive if it reduced its load

by greater than 5% on average during 25% of high price days (i.e., days when prices were more

than $500 for four or more consecutive intervals). 7 A similar, data-driven structure could be

adopted here to ensure that customers with a statistically significant relationship between elevated

prices and lower load are identified as price-responsive and excluded under PURA § 39.170(b)(3),

while customers without that persistent pattern remain eligible. Notably, the Commission and

ERCOT should ensure that any test does not inadvertently exclude loads that curtailed in response

to a request from the Commission or ERCOT for voluntary response during previous extreme

weather events.

       Additionally, it is not clear that large customers who respond to transmission scarcity to

manage 4CP exposure (or a successor methodology) should necessarily be excluded from this new

service. The goal of the service is to procure curtailments that the market would not otherwise

elicit due to price response or participation in other services. Today, 4CP does not reliably align

with net peak load or emergency conditions. The absolute highest demand on the system (i.e. a

4CP interval) often occurs without high wholesale market prices or diminished reserves. As a

result, a customer who responds to 4CP may not necessarily curtail during an emergency, so there

is less likely to be any “double-dipping” as there may be with customers that are price responsive

or participate in other ancillary services. Further, many large industrial loads may exhibit some

limited response to a signal like 4CP, but could provide additional curtailment through the


       7
           ERCOT, Summer 2024 Contracts for Capacity Governing Document (May 29, 2024) at 9.

                                                    8
 proposed service. In other words, customers who have exhibited some 4CP management will not

predictably curtail in response to an extreme weather event and could likely provide distinct and

incremental capability through the service.

       At this time, TIEC does not have any specific recommendations for additional exclusions

beyond those enumerated in PURA § 39.170(b) related to price-responsive loads and loads that

participate in other reliability or ancillary services. The purpose of these exclusions seems to be

to ensure that the service only compensates loads for incremental, verifiable load reductions

directly resulting from the service’s deployment, and not for reductions that would have occurred

anyway. As such, the Commission should tailor any exclusions to capture loads that are already

likely to curtail before or during an extreme weather event.

4.     How should the target quantity, budget, and price be set for the new service?
       As compared to a seasonal procurement with a budget like ERS, or ancillary services that

are procured day-ahead, TIEC acknowledges that an “as-needed” approach can present challenges

for setting target quantities, budgets, and prices. Unlike ancillary services or other reliability

products that are procured and utilized on a regular, recurring schedule, this service is designed to

be activated only in anticipation of extreme emergency conditions—perhaps not even every year.

This can create challenges for Retail Electric Providers (REPs) in modeling and pricing the service

for fixed price contracts, as well as for large customers who are directly exposed to market uplift.

One approach to this challenge could be setting a yearly budget that sets aside funding for the

program, but that is only spent if and when there is a deployment. This budget could be adjusted

over time to address any over- or under-collections based on actual deployments. TIEC is open to

further discussion on this issue but believes this might help minimize costs while providing

predictability to consumers and retail entities.


                                                   9
         When considering pricing and quantity structures during the procurement process, using

the system-wide Value of Lost Load (VOLL) may offer a suitable analytical foundation for

determining the appropriate price and budget for this service. For example, assuming a target

capacity of 500 MW for 3-4 hours of curtailment, an annual budget of approximately $50 million

with an offer cap of $20,000/MWh-$25,000/MWh for the Large Load Demand Management

Service, could be reasonable. This would result in paying out $30 million to $50 million per event

for 500 MW of load to curtail for 3-4 hours.

        For context, this budget is based on the assumption that the Large Load Demand

Management Service offer cap should fall somewhere between the system wide offer cap of

$5,000/MWh and the system-wide VOLL of $35,000/MWh. Large loads would likely not bid into

a service with an offer cap equal to or less than $5,000/MWh because loads could receive the same

net-benefit from curtailing when prices are high. On the other hand, and an offer cap above the

system-wide VOLL may be unnecessarily high as it also captures loads with higher VOLLs that

would likely participate in the service. Further, during the previous VOLL study, the survey results

indicated that medium and large commercial and industrial customers had a VOLL equal to

$22,721/MWh for one hour of unserved energy. 8 This level of compensation would likely reflect

the significant economic sacrifice that these large industrial loads would bear during curtailment

while also remaining within reasonable bounds for consumer cost impacts.

        Additionally, the total budget of $50 million is based on the idea that the service will be

used at most once a year. However, it could be reasonable to increase the yearly budget to $60

million to $75 million, so that additional funds will accumulate if ERCOT needs to deploy the



        8
         Review of Value of Lost Load in the ERCOT Market, Project No. 55837, Staff’s Final Recommendation on
VOLL at 3 (August 22, 2024) (available at: https://interchange.puc.texas.gov/Documents/55837_13_1422000.PDF).

                                                     10
 service multiple times in one year. Given the infrequent nature of this service, the annual budget

does not need to significantly exceed the amount needed to utilize the service in most years.

Further, the budget should be understood not as an expected annual expenditure, but rather as a

ceiling that provides sufficient headroom for the service to function effectively during those rare

periods when it is needed most. This structure ensures that the program can fulfill its statutory

purpose of maintaining reliability during extreme weather events without imposing unnecessary

ongoing costs on the market.

5.     What additional information should the Commission consider in its implementation
       of PURA § 39.170(b)?
       The Commission should consider whether large load customers with onsite backup

generation may participate in the Large Load Demand Management Service. PURA § 37.0561(e)

expressly provides that the large load customers with onsite backup generation are not prohibited

from providing this new service.       As TIEC has noted in the context of other eligibility

considerations, the program’s design should target only those reductions that are incremental to

normal operations and demonstrably attributable to the service’s deployment, rather than

reductions that would have occurred anyway. While these loads are already subject to curtailment

before firm load shed, in some circumstances it may make sense to give ERCOT the ability to

curtail these loads earlier, or to give ERCOT more operational control of such loads under a market

service. If the objective of PURA § 39.170(b) is to maximize the incremental megawatts available

to ERCOT during an anticipated emergency condition, then there may be meaningful value in

making onsite backup generation capacity available earlier in the curtailment sequence than it

would otherwise be deployed. For reference, the capacity associated with large loads with backup

generation only becomes available after ERCOT deploys all available market services except

frequency responsive services. Accessing even some of the demand response from these large


                                                11
 loads earlier, through voluntary participation in the Large Load Demand Management Service,

could provide ERCOT with additional operational flexibility during the critical window between

the identification of an anticipated emergency and the onset of firm load shed. Accordingly, even

where eligibility questions arise, the Commission should consider whether the reliability benefits

of earlier access to that capacity justify inclusion of these customers in the program, subject to

appropriate safeguards to ensure that compensation is directed toward resources that provide

incremental value.

6.     PURA §39.170(a) states: The commission shall require the independent organization
       certified under Section 39.151 for the ERCOT power region to ensure that each
       electric cooperative, transmission and distribution utility, and municipally owned
       utility serving a transmission-voltage customer develops a protocol, including the
       installation of any necessary equipment or technology before the customer is
       interconnected, to allow the load to be curtailed during firm load shed. The electric
       cooperative, transmission and distribution utility, or municipally owned utility shall
       confer with the customer to the extent feasible to shed load in a coordinated manner.
       This subsection applies only to a load interconnected after December 31, 2025, that is
       not: (1) Load operated by a critical load industrial customer, as defined by Section
       17.002; or (2) Designated as a critical natural gas facility under Section 38.074. Should
       the Commission include in this rulemaking a directive implementing PURA
       §39.170(a)?
       The Commission should not include a directive implementing PURA § 39.170(a) in this

rulemaking. In fact, a rulemaking may not be necessary at all because the statutory objectives of

that provision are already being effectuated through the existing ERCOT Protocols and utility

actions.   On May 15, 2025, the Commission approved PGRR115, Related to NPRR1234,

Interconnection Requirements for Large Loads and Modeling Standards for Loads 25 MW or

Greater, which addressed the core mandate of PURA § 39.170(a). Specifically, PGRR115 created

Section 9.2.5 of the Planning Guide, which requires the configuration of each new Large Load

connected at transmission voltage to have remotely controlled breakers that can isolate the load

from the ERCOT System without affecting the transmission lines. In short, this language ensures

that utilities have the necessary equipment to curtail large loads during firm load shed, as required
                                                 12
 by §39.170(a). Additionally, utilities have similarly started implementing this statutory directive

by coordinating with large load customers about how they can identify potential megawatts and

load in a coordinated manner.

       If the Commission determines that a rulemaking is needed to implement PURA

§ 39.170(a), TIEC recommends a separate proceeding.             Project No. 58482 is focused on

developing a new service, the Large Load Demand Management Service. Conversely, this

subsection is an operational and infrastructure-focused requirement related to interconnection

standards, equipment requirements, and utility-customer communication protocols. These two

issues, while superficially related in that both involve large loads and curtailment, are conceptually

and operationally distinct. Combining these two issues into a single rulemaking could create

confusion among market participants regarding the scope and applicability of the resulting rules,

the obligations imposed on utilities versus those imposed on participating customers, and the

relationship between mandatory curtailment during firm load shed and voluntary demand response

service participation. Therefore, if a rulemaking is needed to implement PURA § 39.170(a), it

would be better pursued in a separate proceeding.


                                      III.    CONCLUSION

       TIEC appreciates the opportunity to respond to the Commission’s questions and looks

forward to discussing the issues further with Commission Staff and stakeholders.

                        EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

 •   An “as-needed” service better implements PURA § 39.170(b) because it will only be
     procured for specific extreme weather events. This approach will likely be more effective,
     more cost-efficient, and will maximize participation. TIEC envisions that this service will
     formalize the types of communications and activities that have historically been done on
     an ad hoc, voluntary basis with some industrial sites ahead of emergency conditions.
 •   PURA § 39.170(b)(1) limits the deployment of the large load management service to
     “extreme weather events,” which should be defined as extreme winter storms. Winter
     weather events pose the greatest reliability risk today and are typically discrete and
     identifiable, unlike weather events in other seasons.
 •   TIEC does not believe participation should be limited to loads that require a full 24 hours
     to ramp down safely because it is not required by statute. Instead, qualification should
     focus on whether the load can reduce consumption with advance notice to reach the
     committed curtailment level safely. If the service is only compensated based on actual
     curtailment, there is no need for the same stringent eligibility requirements used for other
     services that receive advance capacity payments.
 •   To determine whether a load is barred from participating because it “curtails in response
     to the wholesale price of electricity,” ERCOT should assess whether the load shows a
     pattern of significant price-responsive curtailment—not isolated instances—and should
     avoid disqualifying loads that reduced usage in response to Commission or ERCOT
     requests for voluntary conservation during past extreme weather events.
 •   An as-needed approach could create challenges for REPs in modeling and pricing the
     service for fixed price contracts, as well as for large customers who are directly exposed to
     market uplift. As a potential solution to improve cost predictability, TIEC suggests a yearly
     adjustable reserve budget that is used only upon deployment.
 •   The system-wide VOLL of $35,000/MWh may offer a suitable analytical foundation for
     the service’s pricing and quantity structure. For example, assuming a target capacity of
     500 MW for 3-4 hours of curtailment, an annual budget of approximately $50 million with
     an offer cap of $20,000/MWh-$25,000/MWh could be reasonable.
 •   The Commission should consider whether large loads with onsite backup generation are
     eligible when SB 6 states that they are not prohibited from providing the service.
 •   A rulemaking may not be necessary to implement PURA § 39.170(a) because its objectives
     are being effectuated through ERCOT Protocols and utility actions. If, however, a
     rulemaking is necessary, it should be done in a separate proceeding.

                                      I.   INTRODUCTION

       Texas Industrial Energy Consumers (TIEC) appreciates the opportunity to provide

feedback on the implementation of PURA § 39.170(b) and the development of a Large Load

Demand Management Service within the ERCOT market.


       TIEC members are among the large electricity users who proposed this service previously

at the Commission and ultimately as part of Senate Bill (SB 6). Many industrial sites are not

flexible and do not typically participate in the wholesale market but are able to reduce their usage

in advance of an emergency event with notice. This notice allows the users to pre-position site

personnel and adjust site operations to achieve an orderly ramp down over a long period, which is

not currently facilitated by existing services with deployment times at thirty minutes or less. TIEC

envisions this service as formalizing the types of communications and activities that have

conditions. Currently, in anticipation of an extreme weather event, the Commission and ERCOT

will often ask industrial customers to voluntarily curtail during the periods when forecasted

conditions look the tightest. These communications often begin several days before an identifiable

weather event-usually a winter storm, but sometimes extreme summer heat). During Winter

                                        II.    COMMENTS

1.     Of the two options described in the attached slides, an as-needed service or a seasonal
       service, which is the better option to implement PURA § 39.170(b) and why?
       TIEC believes an "as-needed" service better implements PURA § 39.170(b) because it will

only be procured for specific extreme weather events. TIEC also anticipates that this approach

will be more effective, more cost-efficient, and will maximize participation.

       As mentioned previously, a central objective of the Large Load Management Service is to

incentivize participation from large loads that would not otherwise participate in the wholesale

market (including price response or ancillary services), but who are able to voluntarily reduce

demand at ERCOT's request in advance of emergency conditions. Under PURA § 39.170, the

service should exclude loads that are price-responsive or that participate in other reliability or

ancillary services. 4 In other words, the service should be designed to attract offers from loads that,

by their nature, do not actively participate in the market but may be willing to respond on a case-

by-case, event-specific basis.



       4 See PURA § 39.170(b)(3)

                                                  3
         An as-needed design is more likely to attract participation from eligible large loads than an

ERS-style service. Many ofthe large load facilities eligible to provide this service operate complex

facilities where the decision to curtail load involves significant operational, safety, and business

considerations. It is more difficult for these customers to commit to curtailing on a seasonal basis,

potentially months in advance. In many ways, a seasonal large load demand service would be

similar to ERCOT' s Summer 2024 Contracts for Capacity RFP, which was ultimately

unsuccessful. 5 For example, both a seasonal service and the RFP entail non-price responsive loads

providing demand-response as needed for a three-month period. While the RFP did not include a

24-hour notice or extreme weather event requirements, it should be illustrative of the limited

number of loads, much less large loads, that may be interested in providing a seasonal demand

response service and are not already participating in ERS. By contrast, an adhoc, event-triggered

approach allows customers to more contemporaneously evaluate their specific circumstances-

including production schedules, operational conditions, and contractual obligations. This practical

flexibility willlikely result in greater participation.

        Additionally, the as-needed model should be more cost-effective. Because procurement

occurs only when ERCOT identifies a need, there is no standing procurement obligation and

therefore no payments would be made for certain seasons or even years. While it may be efficient

to set an annual budget to create more predictability for REPs (as described below), participating

loads would not receive an around-the-clock payment for availability or standby capacity over the

course of an entire season if the service is not needed. Instead, participating loads would be

compensated only if they actually curtail in response to a specific procurement event. By contrast,

two QSEs totaling 21.5 MW of capacity with only 6.5 MW of capacity that could potentially qualify).

 the seasonal model would establish seasonal spend limits and commit resources in advance,

creating budget obligations regardless of whether an emergency event materialized during the

season.

2.        PURA § 39.170(b) states the commission must require ERCOT to develop a reliability
          service to be deployed in the event of an anticipated emergency condition. PURA
          § 39.170(b)(1) states the rules governing the new service must specify the periods
          when the service may be used to assist with maintaining reliability during extreme
          weather events.
          a.      Does PURA authorize ERCOT to deploy the new service in circumstances
                  other than extreme weather events? If yes, what kind of events?

          b.      Should the commission define "extreme weather event" and, if so, how
                  should it be defined?

          PURA § 39.170(b)(1) limits the deployment of the large load management service to

" extreme weather events ." Specifically , PURA states , " the rules governing this service nlust

specify the periods when the service may be used to assist with maintaining reliability during

extreme weather events."6 The directive to "specify the periods when the service may be used"

requires ERCOT to define the particular types of extreme weather events where it may deploy the

service. It is not meant to be a standing tool available at all times or for all categories of grid stress

like other ancillary services but tied to identifiable weather events. Had the Legislature intended

ERCOT to deploy the service in anticipation of any event that may result in entering in an energy

emergency alert, it would not have used such prescriptive language.

          As-needed procurement ahead of an identified weather event (likely an extreme winter

storm) is also the best policy for customers. The ERCOT market already includes a range of

ancillary services and reliability mechanisms designed to address non-weather-related

contingencies.      Extending this new reliability service to those scenarios would effectively



          6 PURA § 39.170(b) (emphasis added).

                                                    5
 repurpose it for conditions that existing market tools are better suited to address. This program' s

intended participants-large industrial loads with significant curtailment lead times and complex

restart procedures-are not well-positioned to serve as a resource for the full range of reliability

events that may arise on the ERCOT system. Confining the service to extreme weather events

preserves a clear and workable boundary to avoid undermining the effectiveness of the service by

overextending its scope and deterring participation.

       At the onset of this program, it would be reasonable to define "extreme weather events" at

least initially, as extreme winter storms. Unlike summer heat, which is predictable, persistent and

well-suited for other types of market response, winter weather events pose the greatest reliability

risktoday and are typically discrete and identifiable. A major winter storm is typically identifiable

in weather forecasts well in advance, facilitating the 24-hour advance notice period contemplated

by the program' s design. Large load customers can plan for and execute an orderly curtailment

when a named or forecasted winter storm is approaching in a way that is not feasible for other, less

predictable reliability events. Further, this type of a bright-line more limited standard would help

ensure that the service is reserved for genuinely extreme conditions and is not diluted through

routine deployment during summer heat.

       TIEC is open to using the service for other types of events, but as an initial step, winter

weather events appear the most suitable. The service could be expanded to other scenarios once

the Commission and ERCOT gain operational experience and develop a clearer understanding of

the system's needs, customer responsiveness, curtailment capabilities, and pricing dynamics.

3.     PURA § 39.170(b)(3) states the rules governing the new service must prohibit
       participation by any large load customer that curtails in response to the wholesale
       price of electricity, as determined by ERCOT, or that otherwise participates in a
       different reliability or ancillary service. PURA § 37.0561(e)-which allows ERCOT
       to direct a large load customer with onsite backup generation to either curtail its load

                                                 6
        or deploy its backup generation under certain circumstances-states that a large load
       customer with onsite backup generation may participate in a service authorized by
       PURA § 39.170(b).
       a.      What type of qualification is necessary to show that it may take a large load
               customer 24 hours to ramp down safely?

       b.      What specific prohibitions not enumerated in PURA § 39.170(b), if any,
               should apply to participation in the new service?

       c.      Should participation in price responsiveness to transmission scarcity such as
               four coincident peak (4CP) or a successor methodology preclude
               participation in the new service?

       d.      Should the commission define "curtailment in response to wholesale price of
               electricity" and, if so, how should it be defined?

       TIEC does not believe it is necessary for a load to show that it takes a full twenty-four

hours to ramp down safely in order to participate. PURA § 39.170(b)(2) requires ERCOT to

provide at least 24 hours' advance notice before deployment, but the statute itself does not require

a 24-hour ramp-down period. In many instances, the actual curtailment will not take twenty-four

hours, but preparatory site activities need to be initiated up to 24-hours in advance. This advance

notice will allow industrial facilities to deploy additional personnel and initiate processes that

allow a reduction in load without compromising safety, product quality, or equipment integrity.

Further, the requirement that participating loads cannot otherwise be price responsive or participate

in ancillary service markets will naturally exclude loads with shorter curtailment capabilities,

driving them into other markets. Consistent with that purpose, qualification should focus on

whether the load can reduce consumption with advance notice to reach the committed curtailment

level safely. This could be memorialized through limited testing or enrollment with a Qualified

Scheduling Entity (QSE) and a straightforward attestation that the site has a protocol in place to

meet the program' s deployment parameters. Again, if the service is only compensated based on

actual curtailments, there is no need for the kind of rigorous eligibility requirements used for other

ancillary or reliability services that receive advance capacity payments.
                                                  7
        To determine whether a load "curtails in response to the wholesale price of electricity" and

is prohibited from participating in the service, ERCOT should look for a pattern of significant

price-response and not isolated instances. In ERCOT's Summer 2024 Contracts for Capacity

Governing Document, ERCOT determined that a site was price-responsive if it reduced its load

by greater than 5% on average during 25% of high price days (i.e., days when prices were more

than $500 for four or more consecutive intervals).7 A similar, data-driven structure could be

adopted here to ensure that customers with a statistically significant relationship between elevated

prices and lower load are identified as price-responsive and excluded under PURA § 39.170(b)(3),

while customers without that persistent pattern remain eligible. Notably, the Commission and

ERCOT should ensure that any test does not inadvertently exclude loads that curtailed in response

to a request from the Commission or ERCOT for voluntary response during previous extreme

weather events.

       Additionally, it is not clear that large customers who respond to transmission scarcity to

manage 4CP exposure (or a successor methodology) should necessarily be excluded from this new

service. The goal of the service is to procure curtailments that the market would not otherwise

elicit due to price response or participation in other services. Today, 4CP does not reliably align

with net peak load or emergency conditions. The absolute highest demand on the system (i.e. a

4CP interval) often occurs without high wholesale market prices or diminished reserves. As a

result, a customer who responds to 4CP may not necessarily curtail during an emergency, so there

is less likely to be any "double-dipping" as there may be with customers that are price responsive

or participate in other ancillary services. Further, many large industrial loads may exhibit some

limited response to a signal like 4CP, but could provide additional curtailment through the



       7 ERCOT , Summer 2024 Contracts for Capacity Governing Document (May 29 , 2024 ) at 9 .

                                                     8
 proposed service. In other words, customers who have exhibited some 4CP management will not

predictably curtail in response to an extreme weather event and could likely provide distinct and

incremental capability through the service.

       At this time, TIEC does not have any specific recommendations for additional exclusions

beyond those enumerated in PURA § 39.170(b) related to price-responsive loads and loads that

participate in other reliability or ancillary services. The purpose of these exclusions seems to be

to ensure that the service only compensates loads for incremental, verifiable load reductions

directly resulting from the service' s deployment, and not for reductions that would have occurred

anyway. As such, the Commission should tailor any exclusions to capture loads that are already

likely to curtail before or during an extreme weather event.

4.     How should the target quantity, budget, and price be set for the new service?
       As compared to a seasonal procurement with a budget like ERS, or ancillary services that

are procured day-ahead, TIEC acknowledges that an "as-needed" approach can present challenges

for setting target quantities, budgets, and prices. Unlike ancillary services or other reliability

products that are procured and utilized on a regular, recurring schedule, this service is designed to

be activated only in anticipation of extreme emergency conditions-perhaps not even every year.

This can create challenges for Retail Electric Providers (REPs) in modeling and pricing the service

for fixed price contracts, as well as for large customers who are directly exposed to market uplift.

One approach to this challenge could be setting a yearly budget that sets aside funding for the

program, but that is only spent if and when there is a deployment. This budget could be adjusted

over time to address any over- or under-collections based on actual deployments. TIEC is open to

further discussion on this issue but believes this might help minimize costs while providing

predictability to consumers and retail entities.


                                                   9
         When considering pricing and quantity structures during the procurement process, using

the system-wide Value of Lost Load (VOLL) may offer a suitable analytical foundation for

determining the appropriate price and budget for this service. For example, assuming a target

capacity of 500 MW for 3-4 hours of curtailment, an annual budget of approximately $50 million

with an offer cap of $20,000/MWh-$25,000/MWh for the Large Load Demand Management

Service, could be reasonable. This would result in paying out $30 million to $50 million per event

for 500 MW of load to curtail for 3-4 hours.


        For context, this budget is based on the assumption that the Large Load Demand

Management Service offer cap should fall somewhere between the system wide offer cap of

$5,000/MWh and the system-wide VOLL of $35,000/MWh. Large loads would likely not bid into

a service with an offer cap equal to or less than $5,000/MWh because loads could receive the same

net-benefit from curtailing when prices are high. On the other hand, and an offer cap above the

system-wide VOLL may be unnecessarily high as it also captures loads with higher VOLLs that

would likely participate in the service. Further, during the previous VOLL study, the survey results

indicated that medium and large commercial and industrial customers had a VOLL equal to

$22,721/MWh for one hour of unserved energy. 8 This level of compensation would likely reflect

the significant economic sacrifice that these large industrial loads would bear during curtailment

while also remaining within reasonable bounds for consumer cost impacts.

        Additionally, the total budget of $50 million is based on the idea that the service will be

used at most once a year. However, it could be reasonable to increase the yearly budget to $60

million to $75 million, so that additional funds will accumulate if ERCOT needs to deploy the




       8 Review of Value of Lost Load in the ERCOT Market, Project No . 55837 , Staff ' s Final Recommendation on
VOLL at 3 (August 22, 2024) (available at: https://interchange.puc.texas.gov/Documents/55837_13_1422000.PDF)

                                                       10
 service multiple times in one year. Given the infrequent nature of this service, the annual budget

does not need to significantly exceed the amount needed to utilize the service in most years.

Further, the budget should be understood not as an expected annual expenditure, but rather as a

ceiling that provides sufficient headroom for the service to function effectively during those rare

periods when it is needed most. This structure ensures that the program can fulfill its statutory

purpose of maintaining reliability during extreme weather events without imposing unnecessary

ongoing costs on the market.

5.     What additional information should the Commission consider in its implementation
       of PURA § 39.170(b)?
       The Commission should consider whether large load customers with onsite backup

generation may participate in the Large Load Demand Management Service. PURA § 37.0561(e)

expressly provides that the large load customers with onsite backup generation are not prohibited

from providing this new service.       As TIEC has noted in the context of other eligibility

considerations, the program' s design should target only those reductions that are incremental to

normal operations and demonstrably attributable to the service' s deployment, rather than

reductions that would have occurred anyway. While these loads are already subject to curtailment

before firm load shed, in some circumstances it may make sense to give ERCOT the ability to

curtail these loads earlier, or to give ERCOT more operational control of such loads under a market

service. Ifthe objective of PURA § 39.170(b) is to maximize the incremental megawatts available

to ERCOT during an anticipated emergency condition, then there may be meaningful value in

making onsite backup generation capacity available earlier in the curtailment sequence than it

would otherwise be deployed. For reference, the capacity associated with large loads with backup

generation only becomes available after ERCOT deploys all available market services except

frequency responsive services. Accessing even some of the demand response from these large


                                                11
 loads earlier, through voluntary participation in the Large Load Demand Management Service,

could provide ERCOT with additional operational flexibility during the critical window between

the identification of an anticipated emergency and the onset of firm load shed. Accordingly, even

where eligibility questions arise, the Commission should consider whether the reliability benefits

of earlier access to that capacity justify inclusion of these customers in the program, subj ect to

appropriate safeguards to ensure that compensation is directed toward resources that provide

incremental value.

6.          PURA §39.170(a) states: The commission shall require the independent organization
            certified under Section 39.151 for the ERCOT power region to ensure that each
            electric cooperative, transmission and distribution utility, and municipally owned
            utility serving a transmission-voltage customer develops a protocol, including the
            installation of any necessary equipment or technology before the customer is
            interconnected, to allow the load to be curtailed during firm load shed. The electric
            cooperative, transmission and distribution utility, or municipally owned utility shall
            confer with the customer to the extent feasible to shed load in a coordinated manner.
            This subsection applies only to a load interconnected after December 31, 2025, that is
            not: (1) Load operated by a critical load industrial customer, as defined by Section
            17.002; or (2) Designated as a critical natural gas facility under Section 38.074. Should
            the Commission include in this rulemaking a directive implementing PURA
            §39.170(a)?
            The Commission should not include a directive implementing PURA § 39.170(a) in this

rulemaking. In fact, a rulemaking may not be necessary at all because the statutory obj ectives of

that provision are already being effectuated through the existing ERCOT Protocols and utility

actions .     On May 15 , 2025 , the Commission approved PGRR115 , Related to NPRR1234,

Interconnection Requirements for Large Loads and Modeling Standards for Loads 25 MW or

Greater, which addressed the core mandate ofPURA § 39 . 170 ( a). Specifically , PGRR115 created

Section 9.2.5 of the Planning Guide, which requires the configuration of each new Large Load

connected at transmission voltage to have remotely controlled breakers that can isolate the load

from the ERCOT System without affecting the transmission lines. In short, this language ensures

that utilities have the necessary equipment to curtail large loads during firm load shed, as required
                                                   12
 by §39.170(a). Additionally, utilities have similarly started implementing this statutory directive

by coordinating with large load customers about how they can identify potential megawatts and

load in a coordinated manner.

       If the Commission determines that a rulemaking is needed to implement PURA

§ 39.170(a), TIEC recommends a separate proceeding.             Project No. 58482 is focused on

developing a new service, the Large Load Demand Management Service.                 Conversely, this

subsection is an operational and infrastructure-focused requirement related to interconnection

standards, equipment requirements, and utility-customer communication protocols. These two

issues, while superficially related in that both involve large loads and curtailment, are conceptually

and operationally distinct. Combining these two issues into a single rulemaking could create

confusion among market participants regarding the scope and applicability of the resulting rules,

the obligations imposed on utilities versus those imposed on participating customers, and the

relationship between mandatory curtailment during firm load shed and voluntary demand response

service participation. Therefore, if a rulemaking is needed to implement PURA § 39.170(a), it

would be better pursued in a separate proceeding.
